Extend the existing Cloudflare DNS integration in the Nxeon platform (/opt/nxeon, Next.js 15, Prisma) so customers can point domains at their server automatically — today Cloudflare is wired ONLY to business-email DNS.

## What already exists (study first; do NOT run git or `npm run build`)
- `lib/cloudflare-dns.ts` — plain server module, Cloudflare v4 REST with a customer API token passed per call: `cfVerifyToken(token)`, `cfFindZoneId(token, zoneName)`, `cfUpsertRecords(...)`, `CloudflareError`. REUSE this; read its signatures carefully (esp. the record shape `cfUpsertRecords` expects).
- `lib/actions-email-hosting.ts` — `saveCloudflareToken(token)` (verifies + stores `encryptSecret` into `User.cloudflareTokenEnc`) and `autoCreateEmailDns(...)` (decrypts, finds zone, upserts MX/SPF/DKIM/DMARC). Copy these patterns exactly (encrypt/decrypt helpers, error handling, `Result` shape).
- `components/customer/EmailDnsSetup.tsx` — the existing "connect Cloudflare + auto-create records" UI, and how it surfaces `cloudflareConnected`.
- `User.cloudflareTokenEnc` already exists — **NO schema change needed and none is allowed** (another agent owns `prisma/schema.prisma` this wave).

## Build these three things
1. **Websites tab: "Point DNS to this server automatically"** — in the control-panel Websites bundle (`lib/actions-websites.ts` + `components/customer/cpanel/*` — find the website-create form/list). When a customer adds a website for `example.com` (or a subdomain), offer a checkbox/button that upserts an **A record** for that hostname → the server's public IP (`Server.ipAddress`, or its `dedicatedIp.address`), proxied=false (must be DNS-only so certbot HTTP-01 validation works — this matters, note it in the UI). Add a server action (e.g. `pointWebsiteDns(websiteId)` or a flag on the create action) that: `requireUser()` + server ownership, requires a connected Cloudflare token (else return a friendly "Connect Cloudflare in Settings first" error), finds the zone for the apex of the hostname, upserts the A record, and reports success/failure. Show the result inline (and that SSL will now be able to validate).
2. **Post-migration: "Point your domains at the new server"** — after a migration completes, the customer still has to move DNS manually (this is the last manual step in an otherwise one-click migration). Add a section to the migration UI (`components/customer/MigrationWizard.tsx` and/or the migration progress/result view — find where the completed-migration summary renders) listing candidate domains, each with a one-click "Point to new server" that upserts the A record to the target server's IP. Sources for the candidate list, in order of what's cheaply available: the customer's `Domain` rows (domains registered with us), plus any hostnames detected in the scan snapshot if the scan captured vhost server_names (check `Migration.items.scan` — only if present; do NOT add new source-scanning). If no candidates, show a simple "enter a domain" input. Requires the Cloudflare token; same friendly prompt if missing.
3. **Account-level "Connected: Cloudflare"** — promote the token from email-only to a visible account integration in **Settings** (`app/dashboard/settings/*`): show connected/not-connected, a paste-token field that calls the existing verify+save path, and a disconnect (clear `cloudflareTokenEnc`). Add `saveCloudflareToken`/`disconnectCloudflare` wrappers in a suitable actions file if reusing the email one is awkward — but do NOT duplicate the Cloudflare client. Explain plainly what scope the token needs (Zone → DNS → Edit) and that we only use it to create records they ask for.

## Constraints
- **No schema change** (`User.cloudflareTokenEnc` suffices). No new deps. Do NOT touch `lib/registrar.ts`, `lib/actions-domains*.ts`, `app/dashboard/domains/*`, `components/customer/Domain*.tsx`, or `prisma/schema.prisma` — another agent owns the domain-transfer work there. Do NOT touch `worker/migrate-real.ts`/`migrate-detect.ts`, mail, billing, backup files. Do NOT run git or `npm run build`.
- Never log or expose the token. Validate the hostname before use. All actions ownership-checked + rate-limited like their neighbours. SANDBOX: don't call Cloudflare — return a synthetic success so staging works.
- Themed to the dark Nxeon UI, honest copy (don't claim DNS propagation is instant; mention it can take a few minutes).
- Write/Edit may time out on a hook — fall back to Bash heredocs and verify.
- Verify ONLY with `cd /opt/nxeon && npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep -v "test/.*test.ts"` (clean for your files).

Report: the three surfaces built, the new actions + their guards, how the A record is upserted (and why proxied=false), the missing-token UX, and sandbox behavior.

# Create your OAuth client

Last updated Jun 3, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/oauth/create-an-oauth-client/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/)

## Prerequisites

To create an OAuth client, you must have one of these roles for the associated account: Super Administrator, Administrator, or OAuth Client Write.

1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard.
2. Select your account.
3. Go to **Manage Account** \> **OAuth clients**.
4. Select **Create client**.
5. Enter the required configuration details:  
  * Client name
  * Response type
  * Grant type
  * Token authentication method
  * Redirect URLs
6. Optional: Add non-required fields.
7. Select **Continue** and define the scopes required for your client.
8. Select **Create client**.
9. Save your **Client ID** and **Client Secret** in a secure location.

[Go to **OAuth clients** ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/oauth-clients)

To create OAuth clients with the Cloudflare API, create an API token with the `OAuth Clients Write` permission.

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/oauth_clients" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
	-d '{
		"client_name": "Cloudflare OAuth Client",
		"grant_types": ["authorization_code"],
		"redirect_uris": ["https://example.com/oauth/callback"],
		"scopes": ["workers-platform.read"],
		"post_logout_redirect_uris": ["https://example.com/logout"],
		"response_types": ["code"],
		"token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_basic",
		"logo_uri": "https://example.com/logo.png",
		"policy_uri": "https://example.com/policy",
		"tos_uri": "https://example.com/tos",
		"client_uri": "https://example.com",
		"allowed_cors_origins": ["https://example.com"]
	}'
```

Note

After you create an OAuth client, Cloudflare displays the client secret if the client requires one. Copy it to a secure location. You cannot view the secret again after you leave the page. If you lose the secret, rotate it to get a new one.

## Select scopes

OAuth scope names correspond to Cloudflare API token permission names. Use the Cloudflare API documentation to identify the permissions your client needs.

When you create or edit an OAuth client, all available scopes are displayed. Search for and select the scopes required for your client.

Fetch the available scopes from the API. Use the scope ID when you create a client through the API.

```bash
curl "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/oauth/scopes" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN"
```

## Supported OAuth flows

Cloudflare OAuth clients support the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow.

Cloudflare does not support Client Credentials, Implicit, Resource Owner Password Credentials, Device Authorization, or other OAuth grant types for third-party clients.

### Choose a flow

Use the following guidance to choose an OAuth flow:

| Client type                                | Flow                                    | Token endpoint authentication                 | PKCE                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Server-side web app or backend service     | Authorization Code with a client secret | client\_secret\_basic or client\_secret\_post | Optional/not required |
| Browser-based, mobile, desktop, or CLI app | Authorization Code with PKCE            | none                                          | Required, S256        |

### Client secret

The Authorization Code flow is intended for secure server-side applications that can protect a client secret from exposure.

* **Use when:** Your OAuth client is a server-side web application or backend service.
* **How it works:** Your client redirects the user to the authorization page. After authorization, Cloudflare returns an authorization code to your backend. Your backend exchanges the code and client secret for an access token.
* **Security note:** Never expose your client secret in client-side code or embed it in mobile client binaries.

### PKCE

Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) extends the Authorization Code flow for public clients, such as mobile or single-page apps, where a client secret cannot be securely stored.

* **Use when:** Your OAuth client is a single-page, mobile, desktop, or CLI application.
* **How it works:** Your application generates a unique code verifier and code challenge for every login request instead of using a static client secret.
* **Security note:** Clients that use PKCE do not need a client secret.

## Private and public clients

New OAuth clients default to private visibility. Private clients can only be authorized by members of the parent Cloudflare account. Public clients allow authorization from any Cloudflare user.

Before you make a client public, complete the required actions and populate the required fields.

### Required fields

* Client name
* Logo
* Client URL
* Scopes

### Required actions

OAuth clients must complete [domain verification](#client-url-domain-ownership-verification) for the client URL before they can be made public.

### Promote a client to public

Caution

Setting a client's visibility to public is permanent. You cannot change the visibility back to private.

1. Go to **Manage Account** \> **OAuth clients**.
2. Open the action menu for your client.
3. Select **Change Visibility**.

[Go to **OAuth clients** ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/oauth-clients)

```bash
curl -X PATCH "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/oauth_clients/$CLIENT_ID" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
	-d '{ "visibility": "public" }'
```

## Client URL domain ownership verification

Cloudflare requires client URL domain ownership verification before a client can become public. If your client is only for private use by members of the account, domain ownership verification is not required.

Caution

After Cloudflare verifies domain ownership, you cannot change the domain of the client URL. You can still update the route for that domain.

Copy the verification code and create a `TXT` record in your DNS configuration with that value. The record must include all text, including the `cloudflare_oauth_client_publisher=` prefix.

Cloudflare polls this DNS record until it is found or until the request times out after two days.

### Restart verification

If the verification process times out, select **Restart verification** in the client action menu.

To restart a failed or timed out verification, send a `PATCH` request with the existing `client_uri` unchanged.

```bash
curl -X PATCH "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/oauth_clients/$CLIENT_ID" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
	-d '{ "client_uri": "https://example.com" }'
```

## Rotate client secrets

Each client can have two secrets. This lets you create a new secret, update your client to use the new secret, and delete the old secret.

1. Go to **Manage Account** \> **OAuth clients**.
2. Open the action menu for your client.
3. Select **Rotate client secret**.
4. Save the new secret in a secure location.
5. After your client uses the new secret, delete the old secret.

[Go to **OAuth clients** ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/:account/oauth-clients)

To check whether a client is in the middle of a secret rotation, look for `has_rotated_secret` in the `GET` response. If the value is `true`, delete the old secret before you create another secret.

#### Create a new secret

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/oauth_clients/$CLIENT_ID/rotate_secret" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN"
```

#### Delete the old secret

```bash
curl -X DELETE "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/oauth_clients/$CLIENT_ID/rotate_secret" \
	-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
	-H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN"
```

Last updated Jun 3, 2026|Copy as Markdown|[View as Markdown](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/oauth/authorizing-an-application/index.md)|[Agent setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agent-setup/)

## Overview

When you authorize a third-party OAuth application, you grant it permission to access specific Cloudflare resources on your behalf. Cloudflare provides tools to view, manage, and revoke these authorizations at any time.

## Authorize a third-party application

When a third-party application requests access to your Cloudflare account, you will see a consent screen that displays:

* **Application name and logo**: The name and branding of the requesting application
* **Publisher domain**: The verified domain of the application publisher
* **Account selection**: Choose which Cloudflare account(s) the application can access
* **Requested permissions**: After selecting the account(s) the application may access, the specific scopes the application is requesting will be displayed before consent is complete. To finish the authorization process, review the permissions the application is requesting and click “**Authorize**”

## View and revoke authorized applications

Application authorizations may be viewed and revoked at any time from the profile page on the Cloudflare dashboard.

1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard.
2. [Go to **Manage OAuth authorizations** ↗](https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=/profile/access-management/authorization)
3. View the list of applications you have authorized.  
  * If you wish to revoke access to an application, click the “Revoke” button for that row

## Account administrator controls

If an account is not available for selection during the consent flow, it may be due to an administrator of that account disabling access to account resources via OAuth.

Account administrators can restrict OAuth applications from accessing account resources via **Manage Account** \> **Members > Settings > Public OAuth App access**.

Caution

This will not prevent existing authorizations account members may already have in place, and will only prevent new authorizations from accessing account resources.

## Domain transfer-in (inbound transfers)

The revenue-generating counterpart to the pre-existing transfer-OUT (unlock + EPP). Customers bring a
domain they own at another registrar INTO Nxeon.

- **Registrar wrappers** (`lib/registrar.ts`, name.com v4 `/v4/transfers`): `checkTransfer(domain)`
  (transferable? price?), `createTransfer(domain, authCode, purchaseCents)`, `getTransfer(domain)`,
  `cancelTransfer(domain)`, `listTransfers()`, plus `transferOutcome()` / `transferStatusLabel()`
  helpers and `transfersAvailable()`. Same Basic auth / dev-host / error handling as the rest of the
  client. Transfer pricing falls back through three sources (the domain's own availability result →
  `:getPricing` → a throwaway probe name on the same TLD) because transfers bill at the TLD's RENEWAL
  rate. In `NXEON_SANDBOX` every wrapper returns synthetic data (names containing `locked` are
  non-transferable, `fail` rejects at submit, and a transfer progresses pendingOwnerApproval →
  pendingRegistry → completed on a compressed few-minute clock) so staging works untouched by name.com.
- **Schema** (additive): `DomainStatus` gains `TRANSFER_PENDING` / `TRANSFER_FAILED`; `Domain` gains
  `isTransferIn`, `transferAuthCodeEnc` (AES-256-GCM via `lib/crypto-box`, scrubbed on completion or
  failure, never logged), `transferStartedAt`, `transferStatus` (raw registrar status), `transferEmail`.
- **Wizard** `/dashboard/domains/transfer` (`DomainTransferInWizard`): domain check → a four-item
  pre-flight gate the customer must tick and the server re-validates (unlocked at the current registrar;
  WHOIS privacy off / auth code obtainable; >60 days since registration or last transfer — ICANN, not
  policy; able to approve the confirmation email) → auth code → review + submit.
- **Money** (`lib/actions-domains-transfer.ts`): server-side re-quote (the client's price is never
  trusted — a drift aborts with the new price), then `createTransfer` at the registrar FIRST and only
  then one `$transaction` doing debit + wallet transaction + PAID invoice + the `Domain` row. Charging
  for an unsubmitted transfer is therefore structurally impossible; double-charging is blocked by the
  in-process submit guard, the UNIQUE `Domain.name` (or a CAS off the retried row's status) inside the
  charging transaction, and name.com refusing a second in-flight transfer. If the debit fails after a
  successful submit we cancel at the registrar and audit-log `domain.transfer_in.uncharged`.
- **Status poll** (`domainTransferInSweep` in `worker/billing.ts`, on the existing 10-minute billing
  cadence): completed → ACTIVE with dates from `domainInfo` and the auth code scrubbed; failed →
  `TRANSFER_FAILED` with the registrar's reason and the wallet credited back; still pending → refresh
  the raw status and nudge the customer (deduped, every 3 days) to approve the losing registrar's email.
  Settlement goes through the CAS-guarded helpers in `lib/domain-transfer.ts`, so a re-run, two workers,
  or a simultaneous customer cancel can never credit twice.
- **Cancel**: `cancelTransferIn` credits the wallet ONLY after the registrar confirms the cancellation —
  never on an assumption — and says so plainly if the registrar refuses (usually because the transfer
  already completed).
- **Copy** is honest throughout: 5–7 days, not instant; the approval email comes from the OLD registrar;
  the 60-day ICANN window; the transfer adds a year on top of the existing expiry.

## Pivot: real OAuth, not pasted tokens

**Endpoints — CONFIRMED** (Cloudflare docs `/fundamentals/oauth/integrate-with-cloudflare/` + their live OIDC discovery doc at `https://dash.cloudflare.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`, fetched today):
- authorize `https://dash.cloudflare.com/oauth2/auth`
- token `https://dash.cloudflare.com/oauth2/token`
- revoke `https://dash.cloudflare.com/oauth2/revoke`
- `grant_types_supported` includes `authorization_code` + `refresh_token`; `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` includes `client_secret_post`/`_basic`; `code_challenge_methods_supported` includes `S256`; `offline_access` is a supported scope.

**Scopes — ASSUMED, not verified.** The resource scope names are only enumerable via `GET https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/oauth/scopes`, which requires an authenticated API token (I confirmed it 400s unauthenticated), and the OIDC doc lists only `openid/offline/offline_access`. Docs say scope names mirror API-token permission names — ours are **"Zone Read"** + **"DNS Write"** (Zone category). Default is `zone:read dns_records:edit offline_access`, in one commented constant block at the top of `lib/cloudflare-oauth.ts`, **overridable via `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_SCOPES`** — so correcting it is an env change, not a code change. Alternate candidate documented inline: `zone.read dns.edit offline_access` (the docs' registration example uses a dotted style, `workers-platform.read`).

## Owner action required
Register an OAuth client (Manage Account → OAuth clients): grant `authorization_code`, response type `code`, token auth `client_secret_post`, redirect URL **`<APP_URL>/api/integrations/cloudflare/callback`**, scopes = Zone Read + DNS Write (+ offline_access). Then set `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` (and `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_SCOPES` if the UI shows different scope strings). Until those are set, `cloudflareOauthConfigured()` is false, the Connect button hides, and the paste-token path still works.

## What was built
**OAuth core** (`lib/cloudflare-oauth.ts`): confidential client, auth-code + PKCE(S256). `GET /api/integrations/cloudflare/start` (requireUser, rate-limited, mints `state` + verifier into a 10-min httpOnly `SameSite=Lax` cookie with the intent and return path) → `GET .../callback` (verifies `state` + that the same user finished it, exchanges the code, stores creds).

**No schema change**: `User.cloudflareTokenEnc` holds an encrypted JSON blob `{accessToken, refreshToken, expiresAt, scope}`; `readStoredCloudflare` sniffs shape — a bare string is still treated as a legacy pasted token and keeps working. `resolveCloudflareToken` refreshes 90s before expiry, re-encrypts, and returns a bearer token; refresh failure returns a friendly "reconnect Cloudflare" rather than throwing. **Every** Cloudflare call goes through it — including `autoCreateEmailDns`, which was still decrypting the raw column and would have broken under OAuth.

**Auto-add on connect**: the cookie carries a validated intent (`email`/`website`/`migration`/`settings`); after consent `runConnectIntent` calls the *same ownership-checked server action the button would have called*, so connecting can never do more than the customer could. Results ride back as `?cf=/?cfdns=/?cfmsg=` and render via `CloudflareResultBanner`.

**Three DNS surfaces**: Websites tab (`pointWebsiteDns`, checkbox on create + per-row "Point DNS"; `listWebsites` now returns `serverIp` + `cloudflareConnected`); post-migration cutover (`getMigrationDnsInfo`/`pointMigrationDns`, candidates from `Domain` rows + websites on the target + hostnames inferred from the *stored* `Migration.items.scan` web-root folder names — the snapshot has no `server_name` field, and I added no new scanning — plus a free-text box; `?migration=<id>` deep-links back after consent); Settings (`CloudflareIntegration` card with connected/disconnect + advanced token paste).

**A record**: `cfUpsertRecords` extended to `"A"` with `proxied` — always written `proxied:false` because HTTP-01 must reach certbot on the box; an existing A at the same name is *updated*, never duplicated, so a repoint can't round-robin old/new. Zone resolution walks hostname suffixes most-specific-first (handles `example.co.uk` and delegated sub-zones).

**Sandbox**: `/start` stores a synthetic blob and runs the intent inline (never leaves the app); all record writes return labelled synthetic success. **Security**: tokens never logged (only a userId on refresh failure) or returned to the client; hostnames re-validated server-side; `next` forced to a relative `/dashboard` path.
